messages.subject: Instability of results with binomial family and Matern model
messages.subject_clean: Instability of results with binomial family and Matern model
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
I am fitting a spatial model with binomial response using Matérn-model to account for spatial autocorrelation, and I have encountered an instability in results when running the same model repeatedly.

I was running my model around 100 times without changing anything, and found out that the coefficients of fixed effects (intercept) change slightly in each run (with one result being significantly more frequent than others). Moreover, when I shuffle the rows of input data frame, the most frequent result is different from those of previous shuffling.

This problem does not occur when omitting the random effect, as well as when using family='gaussian' instead of 'binomial'.

I expect the first issue (different result in each run) to be caused by floating point arithmetic, what bothers me more is the sensitivity to input data frame row order. Is there some specified row order (e.g. by node ID) I shall use to obtain correct results?

Thanks a lot for any help.

Zofie

--------------

My code (data included in the attachement)

# import data

test_data <- read.csv("test_data.csv")

# shuffle rows in data frame

test_data <- test_data[sample(1:nrow(test_data)), ]

# INLA

require(INLA)

## parameters of matern field - range, precision

range=5

precision=-3

shape = 23.36

scale = 0.001

## formula

formula.matern.spatial <- nsuccess ~ 1 + f(ID, model='matern2d',

                                           nrow=10, ncol=10, nu=1,

                                           hyper=list(range=list(initial=log(range), fixed=TRUE),

                                                      prec=list(initial=precision, param=c(shape,scale))))

## fit model 50 times and observe the value of intercept

intercepts <- c()

for (i in 1:50){

  matern.spatial <- inla(formula=formula.matern.spatial,

                         data=test_data,

                         family='binomial',

                         Ntrials=ntrials,

                         verbose=F,

                         control.predictor=list(link=1), # logit link

                         control.inla=list(tolerance=1e-6))

  intercepts <- c(intercepts,matern.spatial$summary.fixed$mean)

}

barplot(table(intercepts))

Hi Elias,
thanks for your comment.
I am not sure if I understood your answer correctly - I don't think that range=log(5) is a large value, but please correct me if it is so.

As for the issue with numerical stability, I was reading this topic ( https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/LB9QdD0rHps ), but this problem does not bother me very much, since after several runs the most frequent result is the correct one I assume.

I am more concerned about the question of input data frame row order. This topic seems similar ( https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/iQcOqUHwxjM ), but it claims the data frame can be ordered in any way, which is not my case. I tested my example with several fixed effects and various order of input data frame rows. It results in various sets of fixed effects to be significant each time. I assume there must be some row order of input data frame, which is correct. Isn't that so?

Thanks,
Zofie

When a model is near non-identifiable you get numerical instability. Parallel computing combines with that in complex ways. Basically, when the model is sensitive to numerical floating point effects surprising things happen, and the solution is to improve the identifiability of the model.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear All

I am working on Generalised Additive Mixed Model (GAMM). I want to implement the B-spline smoothness penalty of Eilers and Marx (1996) using a random walk penalty prior (Lang and Brezger, 2004) for longitudinal count data. The count response is measured for each subject at 20 time points. The time point is the term I want to smooth. Since the subjects are measured at the same time point, I think the basis vectors should stay the same across subjects. Is there a way to implement this in INLA?

Below is my trial. I am afraid I didn’t implement the model well. I even assume an identity penalty matrix because z model didn’t work when I use the random walk penalty.

nyy<-20

  n.sub<-100

  ti<-seq(from=0,to=1,length=nyy)

  data_HPN <-matrix(0,n.sub,nyy)

sig_cluster<-0.5

tru_fun<-(1/3)*dbeta(ti, 20, 5)+(1/3)*dbeta(ti, 12, 12)+(1/3)*dbeta(ti, 7, 30)

  a.i1<-rnorm(n.sub,0,sig_cluster)

for(i in 1:n.sub)

  {

    data_HPN[i,]<-rpois(nyy,lambda =exp(tru_fun+a.i1[i]))

}

y1<-c(data_HPN[1,])  #  HPN

  for (i in 2:n.sub){y1=c(y1,data_HPN[i,])}

time<-c(rep(ti,n.sub))

  id<-rep(1:n.sub,each=nyy)

  dayno.Z <- bspline(time,K=10,bdeg=3,cyclic=1)-mean(bspline(time,K=10,bdeg=3,cyclic=1)[,2])# the #function defined below

id.z<-1:nrow(dayno.Z)

formula_HPN <- y~f(id.z,model="z",Z=ZSpline,constr=T,diagonal=1e-3,initial=3,param=c(1, 0.0005))+

    f(id,model="iid", prior="loggamma", param=c(0.001,0.001))

INLA_HPN = inla(formula_HPN,data=list(y=y1, id.z=id.z,

                                        id=id,ZSpline=dayno.Z),

                  control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE,link=1),family="poisson",

                  control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE))

#B-spline basis function

# -------------------------- Function to construct the Z matrix

bspline <- function(x,K,bdeg,cyclic,xl=min(x),xr=max(x)){

  # x - a covariate vector

  # K - the number of knots

  # bdeg - the degree of the polynomials in the spline

  # cyclic - whether to make the basis periodic

  # xl, xr - minimum and maximum values in the covariate space

  x <- as.matrix(x,ncol=1) # reshape to be a column

  ndx <- K - bdeg # how many knots will be left at the end?

  # as outlined in Eilers and Marx (1996)

  dx <- (xr - xl) / ndx # step size

  t <- xl + dx * (-bdeg:(ndx+bdeg)) # place knots

  # form spline basis of order 0

  T <- (0 * x + 1) %*% t

  X <- x %*% (0 * t + 1)

  P = (X - T) / dx

  B = (T <= X) & (X < (T + dx))

  r = c(2:length(t), 1) # reordering of Indices

  # recursive updating of basis, increasing degree each step

  for (k in 1:bdeg){

    B = (P * B + (k + 1 - P) * B[ ,r]) / k;

  }

  # only return the first K columns

  B <- B[,1:(ndx+bdeg)]

  # convert to periodic basis

  if (cyclic == 1){

    for (i in 1:bdeg){

      B[ ,i] = B[ ,i] + B[ ,K-bdeg+i]

    }

    # get rid of the bits that are being reused

    B <- B[ , 1:(K-bdeg)]

  }

  return(B)

}
Kind regards
Belay

> nyy<-20

>   dayno.Z <- bspline(time,K=10,bdeg=3,cyclic=1)-

> below
> id.z<-1:nrow(dayno.Z)
>
> formula_HPN <- y~f(id.z,model="z",Z=ZSpline,constr=T,diagonal=1e-
> 3,initial=3,param=c(1, 0.0005))+

> INLA_HPN = inla(formula_HPN,data=list(y=y1, id.z=id.z,
>                                         id=id,ZSpline=dayno.Z),
>
> control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE,link=1),family="poisson",
>                   control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE,
> cpo=TRUE))
>
>
> #B-spline basis function
> # -------------------------- Function to construct the Z matrix
> bspline <- function(x,K,bdeg,cyclic,xl=min(x),xr=max(x)){
>   # x - a covariate vector
>   # K - the number of knots
>   # bdeg - the degree of the polynomials in the spline
>   # cyclic - whether to make the basis periodic
>   # xl, xr - minimum and maximum values in the covariate space
>   x <- as.matrix(x,ncol=1) # reshape to be a column
>   ndx <- K - bdeg # how many knots will be left at the end?
>   # as outlined in Eilers and Marx (1996)
>   dx <- (xr - xl) / ndx # step size
>   t <- xl + dx * (-bdeg:(ndx+bdeg)) # place knots
>   # form spline basis of order 0
>   T <- (0 * x + 1) %*% t

>   r = c(2:length(t), 1) # reordering of Indices

>   B <- B[,1:(ndx+bdeg)]
>   # convert to periodic basis
>   if (cyclic == 1){
>     for (i in 1:bdeg){
>       B[ ,i] = B[ ,i] + B[ ,K-bdeg+i]
>     }
>     # get rid of the bits that are being reused
>     B <- B[ , 1:(K-bdeg)]
>   }
>   return(B)
> }

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to reproduce the example 5.4 of the Rue&Martino&Chopin's JRSS paper about cancer incidence (the data seems to be available in INLA package).

Before even trying to figure out how to actually code this up with INLA, I started to wonder how the joint prior precision matrix of the model is computed? In the paper it says that it has dimension of 216 × 15 + 1 = 3241, where 216 is the number of spatial districts, 15 is the number of age groups and 1 is the common intercept. Comparing this with the example in the INLA review paper on https://arxiv.org/pdf/1604.00860.pdf, I don't understand where does this come from? Based on the review paper and my initial intuition I would have assumed the dimensions to be something like 216 (spatial random effect) + 216 (smooth spatial effect) + 15 + 1. Is there some sort of nesting going on or what?

stack, and there use the A matrix for the prediction locations to link
with the mesh.

prediction locations, or even model it) it will work differently.

messages.body_plain:
I've seen this question asked a few times, but without a reproducible example, so I'm not quite sure if/how the following is possible.

I would like to use INLA to implement models with partially missing covariates (i.e. covariate X is observed for n subjects, and not observed for m subjects.) I would like to model the missing values of the covariate, make predictions about the covariate, and use these predictions to model the top level (say, Y). I have tried some version of this below, although it's not quite right, as the missing covariate (x2miss) does not share the same covariate as its observed counterpart (x2). I've tried to follow the "error propagation" technique employed in Muff et al. (2014), though it doesn't quite work because the covariate is not wholly missing, as would be the case in an measurement error model.

library(INLA)

n_miss <- 50
beta_x1 <- 10
beta_x2 <- -4
gamma_x1 <- 2
x1 <- rnorm(100)
x2 <- x1 * gamma_x1 + rnorm(100, 0, 5)
y <- beta_x1 * x1 + beta_x2 * x2 + rnorm(100)
x2[(n_miss + 1):100] <- NA

Y <- matrix(NA, 300, 3)
Y[1:100, 1] <- y
Y[101:200, 2] <- 0
Y[201:300, 3] <- x2
weights <- c(rep(1, 100), rep(-1, 100), rep(1, 100))

df <- data.frame(Y = Y,
                 x1 = c(x1, rep(NA, 200)),
                 x12 = c(rep(NA, 100), x1, rep(NA, 100)),
                 x2 = c(x2, rep(NA, 200)),
                 x2mod = c(rep(NA, 100), 1:100, 1:100),
                 x2miss = c(rep(NA, 50), 51:100, rep(NA, 200)))

out <- inla(Y ~ -1 + x1 + x12 + x2 +
              f(x2miss, copy = 'x2mod',
                hyper = list(beta = list(param = 0, fixed = FALSE))) +
              f(x2mod, weights, model = 'iid', values = 1:100,
                hyper = list(prec = list(initial = -15, fixed = TRUE))),
            family = c('gaussian', 'gaussian', 'gaussian'), data = df)

Furthermore, is it possible to use predictions of covariates if they are NOT gaussian, for instance if the covariate is binary/categorical? I understand it is possible to MAKE predictions of these covariates, but I'm wondering if it's possible to employ them in the model, or if this is something that INLA simply doesn't do. I know the FAQ says "No, INLA has no way to `impute' or integrate-out missing covariates. You have to adjust your model to account for missing covariates. Sometimes, you can formulate a joint model for the data and the covariates, but this is case-specific." I am wondering if/how one would account for missing covariates in the simple example above, and further if/how one would do this if the covariate is categorical. Thanks for any help.

Jonathon

The research into how to use PC priors in your case is not complete. We are working on related problems at the moment.

1 question: You have both alpha_i and b_i, but b_i includes an iid effect. Is this an error?

# What I would do, if I had to solve your problem today
Use separate pc priors for b_i and the other components. So that the prior for the rw2 and the e_ij are "pc.prec".

# Where do you have replicates?
How the priors influence your problem will depend heavily on where you have how many replicates. If you have 100 countries with thousands of patients in each, I am fairly certain any good (i.e. "not bad") prior should give the same result.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

It should be

which was robust. In the process, I came across PC priors and really want to have a try in my current study.

I can usually check for this issue by looking at the logfile :)

> About the inverse gamma prior, I've seen some papers are using them with scaled spatial effect. Those priors are like (1,0.01), (1,0.001) and (1,0.0005). Since they are using INLA, they implemented sensitivity analysis and show the robustness. Based on your experience, is that robustness resulted from scaling? In addition, I wonder if it is possible to scale the precision matrix with some parameter in it, for example, like the smoothing parameter $\rho$ a proper CAR prior.

There is some robustness that comes along from scaling (see Sørbye, S. H. and Rue, H. (2014). Scaling intrinsic Gaussian Markov random field priors in spatial modelling. Spatial Statistics 8 39–51.)

But the use of gamma priors on precisions (or inverse gammas on variances)  is a bad idea.  We have some unpublished [working on it] work that suggests they learn the true parameter at a slower rate than other options.  There is also a very detailed simulation study here:
Klein, N., Kneib, T. et al. (2016). Scale-Dependent Priors for Variance Parameters in Struc- tured Additive Distributional Regression. Bayesian Analysis 11 1071–1106.

> I will try to work on the Half Cauchy prior on standard deviation. I have found some pages regarding on customized prior.

We strongly recommend the exponential prior for reasons outlined at length here: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.4630.pdf.

In our experience, the half-Cauchy's tail is too heavy and can lead to problems.  Gelman no longer recommends it. If for some reason you don't want to use the exponential, a half Student-t distribution with 3 or more degrees of freedom is another option.  (Again, see the simulations of Klein and Kneib).

More discussion on this is here: https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.07487

Hope this helps,

Dan

Hi,
Consider the situation in small area estimation where I have, say, 100 areas but only 60 of them have responses from a survey. Is that possible to build a spatial model to get the estimated responses for area with no observation? To be specific, let y_i is the number of people smoking in area i, then my model would looks like:
y_i ~ Binomial(p_i, m_i)//where m_i is the population
logit(p_i) = intercept + X*beta + b

where X is covariate, beta is fixed effect, and b is random effect following either Besag model, BYM,  BYM2, or BYM2 model.

I have already got some result from when assuming b ~ CAR(rho, C) which is the proper CAR model. Although for some b_i s there is no observation, but the structure of the CAR model can help me get the estimates. I wonder how can use the spatial models like BYM2 to achieve the same purpose?

I noticed that for RW1 and RW2 models, we can have a parameter called values to indicate we want the estimates at those values. But there is no option for spatial structured models. I guess I can have an alternative way to work it out?

Thanks,
Jiang

r = inla(formula, family = "binomial", data = data, Ntrials=c(Ntrials, Ntrials_pred),control.predictor = list(link = 1),
         control.compute = list(config=TRUE))
n_sim = 30000
xx = inla.posterior.sample(n_sim, r)
names_pred = paste('Predictor:', 101:105, sep='')
proportion_sample = numeric(n_sim)
for(i in 1:n_sim){
  eta_sample_i = as.numeric(xx[[i]]$latent[names_pred,])
  p_sample_i = exp(eta_sample_i)/(1+exp(eta_sample_i))
  proportion_sample[i] = sum(p_sample_i * Ntrials_pred)/sum(Ntrials_pred)
}
plot(density(proportion_sample))
mean(proportion_sample)
